prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in this tunable moire system

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B014 as the sole prize part, with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer. After the full first round the case looks stronger to me, not weaker, because the five supporters independently converged on the same three names and the same citation wording, which is built around what was predicted and what was observed, not around the pairing mechanism. The physics is a prediction that can be checked: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model (2011) gave a vanishing Dirac velocity and flat bands at a magic angle, atomistic and tight-binding calculations later confirmed the flat bands, and in 2018 the Jarillo-Herrero group found correlated insulators and superconductivity at the gate-tunable filling of those bands. The phases have since been reproduced by many groups with transport, STM, compressibility and spectroscopy, and the platform opened a field that now includes other moire systems and fractional Chern states. Having read the whole exchange, I also think the phrase in the citation matters: the prediction creates the flat band, but the correlated and superconducting states are the experimental discovery, as Olsson rightly says, and the citation should keep those two steps distinct. This is the pattern I trust in condensed-matter physics: a quantitative model, an independent experimental test, and independent reproduction.
statement.case_against: Two real weaknesses remain and I do not want to hide them. First, attribution: Eva Andrei's STM work on flat-band localisation in twisted graphene is a legitimate independent claim and Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, cannot be named within three people. Second, interpretation: the pairing mechanism is unsettled and twist-angle disorder limits how much fine detail is reproducible, and the field is under ten years old. If an outside expert report shows that Andrei's results established the flat-band physics before and independently of the 2018 experiments, so that the prediction was already confirmed, the credited set would have to be reconsidered; I do not think the packet supports that, but I am recalling the 2010-2017 literature from memory and so cannot exclude it. The open mechanism by itself does not change my view, because the citation does not claim to explain it.

responses.point: Lindroth accepts B014 only if the condensed-matter members can say how secure the interpretation is, since the origin of the superconductivity is debated and samples depend on twist-angle disorder, and she keeps the optical lattice clock first.
responses.response: You asked the condensed-matter members directly, so here is my answer. What is secure: the existence of flat bands near the magic angle, the correlated insulating states at integer fillings, and superconducting domes, which have been seen in several laboratories and with several probes. What is not secure: whether the pairing is phonon-mediated, electronic or both, and how strain and angle disorder shape the phase diagram in detail. A citation for the prediction and the discovery of the phases rests only on the first list. We accept that for earlier prizes where the mechanism was open, and I would hold the citation to that discipline. As for the clock, I would say it differently from round 1: my hesitation is not about reliability, which is excellent, but about whether the committee wants a new regime of matter or a new regime of measurement. I would be comfortable with B013 as my first alternative, and I move it ahead of B041 in my list for that reason. If outside experts show the Sr lattice clock demonstrations were clearly separable between Tokyo and JILA, the case for the pair would be clean.

responses.point: Mehlig reads Andrei's STM evidence as independent support and would resist dropping Bistritzer, so that the choice is Jarillo-Herrero alone for the experiment or a split, and he disagrees with ranking the topological-insulator branch B041 second.
responses.response: On Andrei I move toward your position but not all the way. Her STM flat-band localisation is independent support of the single-particle band structure, and it should be named in the record. It did not show correlated insulators or superconductivity, which are the observations that made the field and are the part of the citation I want to protect. I agree about Bistritzer: the model is a two-author paper and the citation names its mechanism, so removing him would cost the theory half more than adding Andrei would give the experimental half. I also take your point on B041. The 2016 topological prize covers the idea and the allocation among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the omitted BHZ authors is far messier than for twisted graphene, so I have moved it below the lattice clock as my second alternative.

responses.point: Olsson says the flat-band prediction does not itself predict superconductivity, so the experimental discovery is the more original step, and she wants the Andrei priority question settled from the published record and not from memory.
responses.response: I accept your correction and have changed the citation wording to separate the two steps: the prediction is of flat bands at a magic angle, and the discovery is of the correlated insulating and superconducting states. I agree that neither of us should settle Andrei by memory, and I would back a request to the expert reports for a dated list of the STM and transport results from 2010 to 2017 with what each established about flat bands. My own view is that if the answer is that her work confirmed the bands but not the many-body states, it supports a citation that names her work as context, not a fourth name. If the answer is more favourable to her, the realistic cut is to give up one of the theorists, and I would then want the committee to decide that explicitly, because that would change the nature of the prize.

responses.point: Kroll holds that Ye's work on the lattice clock came after and independently of the frequency-comb citation, so a narrow citation tied to the lattice protects the pair, and he asks the experts to check the order of the first Sr lattice clock demonstrations.
responses.response: That is a fair answer to my round-1 concern. Separating lineage from content is what I would do in condensed matter as well, and I accept that Ye's 10^-18 stability and many-body clock physics are not a repeat of the comb recognition. It lowers my objection from overlap with 2005 to the narrower question of whether the lattice clock is a discovery or a capability. I still weight a new phase of matter above a better instrument, so B014 stays first for me, but I would no longer describe B013 as precision engineering only. If B014 fails on the Andrei check, I could support B013 as the lead part with the Katori and Ye pair, and I would back your request for an expert check of the dates.

uncertainties: Whether Andrei's 2010-2017 STM and transport work established flat-band physics independently of the 2018 experiments, and whether that changes the credited names or only the context of the citation
Whether Yuan Cao's role as first author is decisive enough to alter the three-name cut, which I can only judge from memory
Whether the open pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder will be judged a maturity bar by Lindroth and Kroll, and by the outside experts
Whether the optical lattice clock is a discovery of a new regime or a measurement capability, and the order of the first Sr lattice clock demonstrations
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B014 or the named alternatives. I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which affects how I weigh B046 and not any named candidate. My collaborators on atomistic spin dynamics and full-potential codes are not on the shortlist. Updated after round 1: no change to this disclosure.
